{{Short description|Summary of dynamics of a stochastic process}}
The '''Onsager–Machlup function''' is a function that summarizes the dynamics of a [[stochastic process#Continuous time and continuous state space|continuous stochastic process]]. It is used to define a probability density for a stochastic process, and it is similar to the [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian]] of a [[dynamical system]]. It is named after [[Lars Onsager]] and {{interlanguage link|Stefan Machlup|de}} who were the first to consider such probability densities.<ref>Onsager, L. and Machlup, S. (1953)</ref>

The dynamics of a continuous stochastic process {{mvar|X}} from time {{math|''t'' {{=}} 0}} to {{math|''t'' {{=}} ''T''}} in one dimension, satisfying a [[stochastic differential equation]]

:<math> dX_t = b(X_t)\,dt + \sigma(X_t)\,dW_t </math>

where {{mvar|W}} is a [[Wiener process]], can in approximation be described by the [[probability density function]] of its value {{math|''x<sub>i</sub>''}} at a finite number of points in time {{math|''t<sub>i</sub>''}}:

:<math> p(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \left( \prod^{n-1}_{i=1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma(x_i)^2\Delta t_i}} \right) \exp\left(-\sum^{n-1}_{i=1} L\left(x_i,\frac{x_{i+1}-x_i}{\Delta t_i}\right) \, \Delta t_i \right) </math>

where

:<math> L(x,v) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{v - b(x)}{\sigma(x)}\right)^2 </math>

and {{math|Δ''t<sub>i</sub>'' {{=}} ''t''<sub>''i''+1</sub> − ''t<sub>i</sub>'' > 0}}, {{math|''t''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} 0}} and {{math|''t<sub>n</sub>'' {{=}} ''T''}}. A similar approximation is possible for processes in higher dimensions. The approximation is more accurate for smaller time step sizes {{math|Δ''t<sub>i</sub>''}}, but in the limit {{math|Δ''t<sub>i</sub>'' → 0}} the probability density function becomes ill-defined, one reason being that the product of terms

:<math>\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma(x_i)^2\Delta t_i}}</math>

[[limit of a sequence#Infinite limits|diverges to infinity]]. In order to nevertheless define a density for the continuous stochastic process {{mvar|X}}, [[ratio]]s of probabilities of {{mvar|X}} lying within a small distance {{mvar|ε}} from [[smooth function|smooth]] curves {{math|''φ''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''φ''<sub>2</sub>}} are considered:<ref>Stratonovich, R. (1971)</ref>

:<math>\frac{P\left( \left |X_t - \varphi_1(t) \right| \leq \varepsilon \text{ for every }t\in[0,T] \right)}{P\left( \left |X_t - \varphi_2(t) \right | \leq \varepsilon \text{ for every }t\in[0,T] \right)} \to \exp\left(-\int^T_0 L \left (\varphi_1(t),\dot{\varphi}_1(t) \right ) \, dt + \int^T_0 L \left (\varphi_2(t),\dot{\varphi}_2(t) \right) \, dt \right)</math>

as {{math|''ε'' → 0}}, where {{mvar|L}} is the '''Onsager–Machlup function'''.

==Definition==
Consider a {{mvar|d}}-dimensional [[Riemannian manifold]] {{mvar|M}} and a [[diffusion process]] {{math|''X'' {{=}} {''X<sub>t</sub>'' : 0 ≤  ''t'' ≤ ''T''} }} on {{mvar|M}} with [[infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]] {{math|{{sfrac|1|2}}Δ<sub>''M''</sub> + ''b''}}, where {{math|Δ<sub>''M''</sub>}} is the [[Laplace–Beltrami operator]] and {{mvar|b}} is a [[vector field]]. For any two [[smooth function|smooth]] curves {{math|''φ''<sub>1</sub>, ''φ''<sub>2</sub> : [0, ''T''] → ''M''}},

:<math>\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0} \frac{P\left( \rho(X_t,\varphi_1(t)) \leq \varepsilon \text{ for every }t\in[0,T] \right)}{P\left( \rho(X_t,\varphi_2(t)) \leq \varepsilon \text{ for every }t\in[0,T] \right)} = \exp\left( -\int^T_0 L \left (\varphi_1(t),\dot{\varphi}_1(t) \right ) \, dt  +\int^T_0 L \left (\varphi_2(t),\dot{\varphi}_2(t) \right ) \, dt  \right)</math>

where {{mvar|ρ}} is the [[metric (mathematics)|Riemannian distance]], <math>\scriptstyle \dot{\varphi}_1, \dot{\varphi}_2</math> denote the first [[derivative]]s of {{math|''φ''<sub>1</sub>, ''φ''<sub>2</sub>}}, and {{mvar|L}} is called the '''Onsager–Machlup function'''.

The Onsager–Machlup function is given by<ref>Takahashi, Y. and Watanabe, S. (1980)</ref><ref>Fujita, T. and Kotani, S. (1982)</ref><ref>Wittich, Olaf</ref>

:<math> L(x,v) = \tfrac{1}{2}\|v-b(x)\|_x^2 +\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{div}\, b(x) - \tfrac{1}{12}R(x), </math>

where {{math|{{!!}} ⋅ {{!!}}<sub>''x''</sub>}} is the Riemannian norm in the [[tangent space]] {{math|''T<sub>x</sub>''(''M'')}} at {{mvar|x}}, {{math|div ''b''(''x'')}} is the [[divergence]] of {{mvar|b}} at {{mvar|x}}, and {{math|''R''(''x'')}} is the [[scalar curvature]] at {{mvar|x}}.

==Examples==
The following examples give explicit expressions for the Onsager–Machlup function of a continuous stochastic processes.

===Wiener process on the real line===
The Onsager–Machlup function of a [[Wiener process]] on the [[real line]] {{math|'''R'''}} is given by<ref>Ikeda, N. and Watanabe, S. (1980), Chapter VI, Section 9</ref>

:<math>L(x,v)=\tfrac{1}{2}|v|^2.</math>

Proof: Let {{math|''X'' {{=}} {''X<sub>t</sub>'' : 0 ≤ ''t'' ≤ ''T''} }} be a Wiener process on {{math|'''R'''}} and let {{math|''φ'' : [0, ''T''] → '''R'''}} be a twice [[differentiable curve]] such that {{math|''φ''(0) {{=}} ''X''<sub>0</sub>}}. Define another process {{math|''X<sup>φ</sup>'' {{=}} {''X<sub>t</sub><sup>φ</sup>'' : 0 ≤ ''t'' ≤ ''T''} }} by {{math|''X<sub>t</sub><sup>φ</sup>'' {{=}} ''X<sub>t</sub>'' − ''φ''(''t'')}} and a [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] {{math|''P<sup>φ</sup>''}} by

:<math> P^\varphi = \exp\left( \int^T_0\dot{\varphi}(t) \, dX^\varphi_t + \int^T_0\tfrac{1}{2} \left |\dot{\varphi}(t) \right |^2 \, dt \right) \, dP. </math>

For every {{math|''ε'' > 0}}, the probability that {{math|{{!}}''X<sub>t</sub>'' − ''φ''(''t''){{!}} ≤ ''ε''}} for every {{math|''t'' ∈ [0, ''T'']}} satisfies

:<math> \begin{align}
P \left ( \left |X_t-\varphi(t) \right |\leq\varepsilon \text{ for every }t\in[0,T] \right ) &=P\left ( \left |X^\varphi_t \right|\leq\varepsilon \text{ for every }t\in[0,T] \right) \\
&=\int_{\left \{ \left |X^\varphi_t \right |\leq\varepsilon\text{ for every }t\in[0,T] \right\}} \exp\left( -\int^T_0\dot{\varphi}(t) \, dX^\varphi_t -\int^T_0\tfrac{1}{2}|\dot{\varphi}(t)|^2 \, dt \right) \, dP^\varphi.
\end{align}</math>

By [[Girsanov theorem|Girsanov's theorem]], the distribution of {{math|''X<sup>φ</sup>''}} under {{math|''P<sup>φ</sup>''}} equals the distribution of {{mvar|X}} under {{mvar|P}}, hence the latter can be substituted by the former:

:<math>P(|X_t-\varphi(t)|\leq\varepsilon \text{ for every }t\in[0,T])=\int_{\left \{ \left |X^\varphi_t \right |\leq\varepsilon\text{ for every }t\in[0,T] \right\}} \exp\left( -\int^T_0\dot{\varphi}(t) \, dX_t -\int^T_0\tfrac{1}{2}|\dot{\varphi}(t)|^2 \, dt \right) \, dP.</math>

By [[Itō's lemma]] it holds that

:<math> \int^T_0\dot{\varphi}(t) \, dX_t = \dot{\varphi}(T)X_T - \int^T_0\ddot{\varphi}(t)X_t \, dt, </math>

where <math>\scriptstyle \ddot{\varphi}</math> is the second derivative of {{mvar|φ}}, and so this term is of order {{mvar|ε}} on the event where {{math|{{!}}''X<sub>t</sub>''{{!}} ≤ ε}} for every {{math|''t'' ∈ [0, ''T'']}} and will disappear in the limit {{math|''ε'' → 0}}, hence

:<math> \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0} \frac{P(|X_t-\varphi(t)|\leq\varepsilon \text{ for every }t\in[0,T])}{P(|X_t|\leq\varepsilon\text{ for every } t \in [0,T])} =\exp\left( -\int^T_0\tfrac{1}{2}|\dot{\varphi}(t)|^2 \, dt \right).</math>

===Diffusion processes with constant diffusion coefficient on Euclidean space===
The Onsager–Machlup function in the one-dimensional case with constant [[Itō diffusion|diffusion coefficient]] {{mvar|σ}} is given by<ref>Dürr, D. and Bach, A. (1978)</ref>

:<math>L(x,v)=\frac{1}{2}\left|\frac{v-b(x)}{\sigma}\right|^2 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{db}{dx}(x). </math>

In the {{mvar|d}}-dimensional case, with {{mvar|σ}} equal to the [[Identity matrix|unit matrix]], it is given by<ref>Ikeda, N. and Watanabe, S. (1980), Chapter VI, Section 9</ref>

:<math> L(x,v)=\frac{1}{2}\|v-b(x)\|^2 + \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{div}\, b)(x), </math>

where {{math|{{!!}} ⋅ {{!!}}}} is the [[Euclidean norm]] and

:<math>(\operatorname{div}\, b)(x) = \sum_{i=1}^d \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} b_i(x).</math>

==Generalizations==
Generalizations have been obtained by weakening the differentiability condition on the curve {{mvar|φ}}.<ref>Zeitouni, O. (1989)</ref> Rather than taking the maximum distance between the stochastic process and the curve over a time interval, other conditions have been considered such as distances based on completely convex norms<ref>Shepp, L. and Zeitouni, O. (1993)</ref> and Hölder, Besov and Sobolev type norms.<ref>Capitaine, M. (1995)</ref>

==Applications==
The Onsager–Machlup function can be used for purposes of reweighting and [[Sampling (statistics)|sampling]] trajectories,<ref>Adib, A.B. (2008).</ref>
as well as for determining the most probable trajectory of a diffusion process.<ref>Adib, A.B. (2008).</ref><ref>Dürr, D. and Bach, A. (1978).</ref>
